title: Crossbar Theorem
statement: If ray AD lies inside \(\angle BAC\) of triangle ABC, then ray AD meets segment BC at a point E between B and C.
theoremLatex: \begin{gathered}\text{If }\overrightarrow{AD}\text{ lies inside }\angle BAC, \\ \text{then }\overrightarrow{AD}\text{ meets }\overline{BC}\text{ at }E,\text{ with }E\text{ between }B\text{ and }C.\end{gathered}
summary: If a ray starts at a vertex of a triangle and stays inside that vertex angle, then the ray must leave the triangle through the opposite side.
proofIdea: Extend AB past A to Q and apply plane separation to triangle QBC. The line through A and D meets side QB at A, so Pasch's triangle-crossing conclusion says it must meet QC or BC. The same-side part of angle interior rules out QC, leaving BC as the only possible crossing side.
explorationPrompt: Move D inside the fixed triangle and track where ray AD reaches side BC. Then step through the proof to see why QC is the only branch that gets eliminated.

proofSteps.title: Extend AB past A to Q
proofSteps.detail: By the Order Axioms, line AB can be extended past A to a point Q with A between Q and B. This turns the original triangle into the larger triangle QBC while keeping A on side QB.

proofSteps.title: Use plane separation on triangle QBC
proofSteps.detail: The line through A and D meets side QB of triangle QBC at A, and because D is inside the original angle, that line does not pass through Q, B, or C. Plane Separation, in Pasch form, says that a line entering triangle QBC through side QB must also meet either side QC or side BC.

proofSteps.title: Rule out the QC branch
proofSteps.detail: Because ray AD lies inside ∠BAC, point D is on the same side of line AC as B. Point Q lies on the opposite side of AC from B, and every point of segment QC except C stays on Q's side of AC. So ray AD cannot meet QC.

proofSteps.title: Conclude the hit lies on BC
proofSteps.detail: The QC option is impossible, so the remaining Pasch intersection is a point E on BC. Since E is also on ray AD, E lies between B and C on side BC.

corollaries.title: Corollary: triangle-crossing line form
corollaries.statement: If a line meets one side of a triangle at an interior point and avoids the vertices, then it meets exactly one other side of the triangle.
corollaries.theoremLatex: \begin{gathered}\text{A line meets side }AB\text{ at point }P\text{ between }A\text{ and }B \\ \text{The line avoids vertices }A, B, C \\ \text{Then it meets exactly one of sides }AC\text{ or }BC\end{gathered}
corollaries.proof: Let the line meet side AB at an interior point P. Exactly one ray from P lies on the same side of AB as C, so exactly one ray enters the triangle interior. Segment PC divides that interior near P into the two disjoint angles ∠APC and ∠CPB, so the inward ray lies inside exactly one of them. If it lies inside ∠APC, apply the Crossbar Theorem in triangle APC to show that ray meets side AC. If it lies inside ∠CPB, apply the theorem in triangle PBC to show that ray meets side BC. These cases are exclusive, so the line meets exactly one other side of triangle ABC.
corollaries.proofLatex: \begin{gathered}\text{Exactly one ray from }P\text{ enters the triangle.} \\ \text{That ray lies inside either }\angle APC\text{ or }\angle CPB. \\ \text{Apply Crossbar in triangle }APC\text{ or }PBC. \\ \text{The cases are exclusive, so only one other side is met.}\end{gathered}

historicalContext.title: Pasch's triangle-crossing insight
paragraphs: Moritz Pasch emphasized that a line crossing a triangle cannot be justified by a picture alone; it depends on explicit order and same-side principles.
The crossbar theorem is one clean consequence of that shift. It turns angle interior and plane separation into a rigorous reason that a ray from a vertex must hit the opposite side.
